title: Linear algebra, from arrows to vibration modes
hook: Two equal masses on three equal springs shudder in a tangle. A ship's propulsion shaft twists to and fro in the same kind of way, and engineers work it out with the same sums. Which two simple swings hide inside the masses' shudder, and what sets how fast each one goes?
oneBreath: Mix a few arrows in any amounts and you reach a line, a plane or all of space, and an arrow's numbers are just the amounts of each arrow in the set you chose to measure with. Lines and planes in space are written the same way, and every matrix has a set of points it can reach and a set it crushes to nothing, which together say how many answers a system has. Most matrices also have a few directions they only stretch, and measuring along those turns a hundred repeated steps into one power and splits two linked things, such as two tanks or two masses on springs, into simple motions that each keep their own rate.

ideas.title: Which points two arrows reach: span and independence
ideas.oneLine: The span of some arrows is every point their mixes can reach, and they are independent when each one adds a direction the others cannot.

ideas.title: One arrow, two grids: change of basis
ideas.oneLine: An arrow's numbers are the amounts of each basis arrow, and a matrix whose columns are the new basis arrows converts between two grids.

ideas.title: Lines and planes in space
ideas.oneLine: A line in space is a point plus any amount of one direction, and a plane is a point plus a normal arrow, giving ax + by + cz = d.

ideas.title: What a matrix reaches and what it crushes: rank and null space
ideas.oneLine: A matrix's column space is everything it can reach and its null space everything it crushes to zero, and their sizes decide how many answers Ax = b has.

ideas.title: Directions that only stretch: eigenvalues and eigenvectors
ideas.oneLine: An eigenvector is a direction a matrix only stretches, by a factor called its eigenvalue, found by solving det(A − λI) = 0 and then (A − λI)v = 0.

ideas.title: Diagonalising: the same step, again and again
ideas.oneLine: A matrix with enough eigenvectors is a plain stretch on their grid, P⁻¹AP = D, so n repeated steps are just Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹.

ideas.title: Coupled change: two tanks and two masses
ideas.oneLine: Linked rates written as x′ = Ax split along the eigenvectors into separate motions, so two tanks or two masses on springs move as a sum of modes.

calibration.q: On a flat deck you can push a crate 2 m east and 1 m north, or 4 m west and 2 m south, any number of times, even part-times. Where can it end up?
options: Only somewhere on one straight line
Only due east or due west of the start
calibration.why: The second push is exactly minus two of the first, so both run along the same line. Any mix of them stays on that line. Two different-looking pushes reach the whole deck only when they point along different lines.

calibration.q: A deck plan is drawn on a grid of 2 m squares. A bollard stands 6 m east and 4 m north of the grid's corner. What are its grid numbers?
calibration.why: Each grid step is 2 m, so 6 m east is 3 steps and 4 m north is 2 steps. The numbers count grid steps, not metres, and multiplying by 2 instead of dividing gives 12 and 8.
